extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, Congressional staff, USPTO policymakers, and stakeholders evaluating S.1145 patent reform
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of statutory and procedural standards proposed in S.1145 regarding willful infringement, prior user rights, notice/marking, post-grant review, third-party submissions, publication, and venue. Targeted to those applying or interpreting the bill's provisions in U.S. patent practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness: judge decides willfulness after validity and infringement findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike current practice where willfulness can be pleaded at the outset and decided by a jury, willfulness will now be decided by the judge and only after finding that the patent was valid and infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural change is intended to reduce unwarranted allegations of willfulness and unnecessary costly discovery by deferring willfulness determinations until after the court has found validity and infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness burden of proof: clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to new paragraph (e)(2) of section 284, willfulness must be demonstrated by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elevates the standard of proof for willfulness findings compared to permissive pleading under previous practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness pleading particularity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusive allegations no longer suffice; under subparagraph (e)(2)(A), the patent holder must allege acts of infringement sufficient to give the alleged infringer an objectively reasonable apprehension of suit and must plead with particularity which products or processes allegedly infringe which claims, as well as the basis for such a belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires detailed factual pleading to support willfulness claims, reducing vague or boilerplate willfulness allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness grounds: intentional copying and continued infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Subparagraph (e)(2)(B) permits a finding of willfulness if the infringer intentionally copied the patented invention with knowledge it was patented. Subparagraph (e)(2)(C) permits such a finding if the infringer continued to engage in infringing conduct after a court already found the party to be infringing the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies discrete factual bases that can support willfulness (copying with knowledge; post-adverse-court-conduct).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good faith defense to willfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (e)(3) provides a good faith defense: an infringer can establish good faith through reasonable reliance on the advice of counsel; evidence that the infringer sought to modify its conduct to avoid infringement once it had discovered the patent; or other evidence a court may find sufficient. The decision not to present evidence of advice of counsel is not relevant to determination of willful infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates a meaningful, evidence-based defense to counter enhanced damages for willfulness and protects reliance on counsel and remedial steps as exculpatory evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior user rights: affiliates allowed and USPTO study
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendment clarifies that 'affiliates' of the user may assert the prior user defense; affiliates include those who caused or controlled the acts that were performed that give rise to the defense. The Director of the USPTO is instructed to conduct and provide to Congress a study with recommendations on prior user rights within two years of enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrows initial bill proposal (which would have extended prior user rights to all patents) to a more limited change expanding who may assert the defense and directing a study on broader reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and marking: constructive notice and recovery of damages
rubrics_metrics.description: For patented 'articles,' a patent holder must give an alleged infringer notice of the claimed infringement, and the infringer must continue to infringe before the patent holder may succeed in a suit for damages. Constructive notice is possible by 'marking' any patented article that the patent holder (or its licensee) makes, uses, sells or imports; failure to appropriately mark an article can preclude the recovery of damages until notice is effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes actual notice (affirmative communication, including suit) from constructive notice by marking; failure to mark delays accrual of damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception for processes/method patents and damages accrual reduction for unmarkable patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents on methods or processes are not 'articles' and cannot be marked; under current law a patent holder of such a patent may recover up to six years of past damages. The change in Section 4 reduces the maximum period for which damages can be recovered for patents not covered by marking requirements from 6 years to 2 years from the date of actual notice, if infringement is proven during that period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims to reduce disparity between markable and unmarkable patents and to protect unknowing infringers of unmarkable patents by shortening retrospective damages exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date for Section 4 amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: The amendments in Section 4 of the Act shall apply to any civil action commenced on or after the date of enactment of the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal scope clarifies that the new willfulness, notice/marking, and damages rules apply only to actions filed after enactment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement of inter partes reexamination with Post-Grant Review (PGR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 creates a new post-grant review (PGR) system for United States patents, replacing and eliminating inter partes reexamination, in a new chapter 32 in title 35. Ex parte reexamination (patentee-requested) is retained but third parties may no longer request ex parte reexamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGR is intended as a 'clean start' to provide a quick, inexpensive, reliable administrative alternative to district court litigation for challenging patent validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGR initiation windows: first window, second window, and consent
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three ways to initiate a PGR proceeding: a first-window petition (within 12 months of issuance), a second-window petition (throughout life of the patent subject to limits), and petitions based on the patentee's consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The windows differ procedurally and substantively; first window is designed as extension of examination, second window imposes standing/timing limits to avoid harassment and preserve business certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-window PGR standards: timing and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: In a first window PGR, the petition must be filed within 12 months of the patent's issuing. The presumption of validity for the patent does not apply, and the petitioner has the burden of proving invalidity by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-window is crafted as a near-issuance review where the usual presumption is relaxed to mirror examination and to encourage early post-issuance challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-window PGR standards: standing, timing, and burdens of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: In the second window, a PGR petition may be filed throughout the life of the patent only if (i) the continued existence of the challenged patent claim is likely to cause the petitioner significant economic harm, and (ii) the petitioner files the petition within 12 months after receiving notice of infringement. The presumption of validity applies; the petitioner may challenge a patent based on any defense available in district court, but the existence/authentication/availability/scope of evidence offered to establish invalidity must be established by clear and convincing evidence, and if such predicates are established, invalidity is proven only if the persuasive force of such facts demonstrates invalidity by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits second-window challenges to parties with a stake and raises evidentiary predicates to deter frivolous or harassment filings while preserving broad substantive grounds available in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGR estoppel and 'one bite at the apple' rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Every petition to institute a PGR must raise a substantial new question of patentability. The same party who has filed a PGR petition regarding any claim in a patent may not file another PGR on the same patent. Once a petitioner has challenged the validity of a patent through a PGR, that party may not challenge validity in a court proceeding based on any ground it raised during the PGR. Conversely, a party who has challenged the validity of a patent in court may not file a PGR petition on any grounds they raised, or could have raised, in the district court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to prevent serial challenges and harassment and to coordinate estoppel between administrative PGR and district court litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial new question of patentability standard for instituting PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: Every petition to institute a PGR must raise a 'substantial new question of patentability'; the Director will prescribe regulations regarding the standard necessary to show that this exists (the standard is the same as required to initiate a reexamination under current law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elevated during mark-up to encourage only meaningful challenges; regulatory definition to be provided by Director.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim amendment limits during PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: After a PGR is initiated, the patent holder has one opportunity as a matter of right to amend the claims, and may only amend the claims subsequently on motion and a showing of good cause. No amendment during a PGR proceeding may enlarge the scope of a claim or add new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits narrow claim corrections while preventing broadenings or new subject matter that could unfairly prejudice others.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGR procedure, timelines, decisionmakers, appeals, and public access
rubrics_metrics.description: PGR proceedings are conducted in the first instance by three Patent Board judges (not first by an examiner). The USPTO must complete its work on a PGR within one year in most cases and within 18 months only when additional time is justified. Any party dissatisfied with a Board PGR decision may appeal to the Federal Circuit, and all parties to the PGR proceeding may participate in such an appeal. PGR proceedings are open to the public unless determined otherwise by the Patent Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifts initial decisionmaking to panels of judges to reduce pendency, allows appellate review, and increases transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO regulatory duties and anti-harassment measures for PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director is instructed to issue regulations developing rules and procedures governing PGR proceedings and is admonished to ensure that regulations forbidding and penalizing harassment are enacted and enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory framework expected to streamline proceedings, ensure transparency, and deter abusive filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGR applicability and patent eligibility by filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: The PGR process shall take effect one year after enactment. After that time, first-window PGR petitions may be filed against any patent, but second-window PGR petitions (and consented petitions) may only be filed on patents that issue based on applications filed after November 29, 1999.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phase-in and eligibility rules limit second-window access to patents analogous to those eligible for prior inter partes reexamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of the old reexamination system motivating PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: Reexamination under the former system could only be based on documentary prior art (not prior use or prior sales); challengers could not raise Sec. 101 or Sec. 112-based attacks (utility/eligibility, indefiniteness/enablement/written description); third parties had limited roles and losers initially lacked appeal rights; serial reexaminations and assignment to original examiners added delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These structural limitations and long pendency were cited as reasons reexamination was an ineffective alternative to litigation, motivating the shift to PGR.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18-month publication of patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 7 eliminates previous exemptions and requires that all applications filed at the USPTO be published within 18 months of filing (removing exemption for applications that certify no foreign filing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication promotes disclosure, reduces 'submarine' patents, increases business certainty, and allows the public to learn of pending claims earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party submissions after publication: allowed explanations of relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: After an application is published, third parties may submit prior art; Section 7 permits those third parties to make statements concerning the relevance of the patents, patent applications, and other printed publications they bring to the USPTO's attention. Previously such submissions were limited to patents/publications and could not include explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing explanatory statements increases the value of third-party submissions to examiners and may encourage more useful prior-art submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue jurisprudence and forum shopping concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific patent venue provision exists (28 U.S.C. Sec. 1400), but Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., VE Holding Corp. v. Johnson Gas Appliance Co. and Beverly Hills Fan Co. v. Royal Sovereign Corp.) have expanded venue by importing general venue standards and personal jurisdiction rules, effectively allowing patent suits anywhere an infringing product can be found and producing concentration of cases in a few districts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the background problem of forum shopping and the narrowing of meaningful geographic limitations on patent venue; provides context for proposed venue-related reforms.
